tEn: Evan Spiegel on Building Snapchat and Battling Meta
tZh: 埃文·斯皮格尔谈打造Snapchat与对抗Meta
sEn: Snapchat founder Evan Spiegel reflects on early secrecy, Meta's 'Poke' ripoff, and his evolution as a leader.
sZh: Snapchat创始人埃文·斯皮格尔回顾早期保密策略、Meta的“Poke”抄袭事件，以及他作为领导者的成长。

consensus.en: Early secrecy at Snap was a huge mistake; internal transparency is essential for culture, vision, and getting the best ideas.
consensus.zh: 早期Snap的保密是个大错误；内部透明对文化、愿景和获取最佳创意至关重要。

consensus.en: Steve Jobs inspired Spiegel: great design means making things work beautifully, not just making them look beautiful.
consensus.zh: 史蒂夫·乔布斯启发了他：伟大的设计是让产品运行得优雅，而不仅仅是看起来漂亮。

consensus.en: The whole game is how quickly you change your mind once wrong; reward speed of admitting mistakes.
consensus.zh: 关键在于发现自己错了之后能多快改变想法；要奖励快速承认错误的行为。

consensus.en: The goal is to make computing more human, bringing people together rather than separating them into single-player experiences.
consensus.zh: 目标是让计算更人性化，让人们聚在一起，而不是让他们陷入单人体验。

consensus.en: Social media should optimize for human connection and relationships, not competition through likes and comments.
consensus.zh: 社交媒体应优化人与人之间的连接和关系，而不是通过点赞和评论来鼓励竞争。

consensus.en: Not giving up is the defining trait of successful founders; resilience matters more than any silver bullet.
consensus.zh: 不放弃是成功创始人的核心特质；韧性比任何捷径都重要。

contrarian.en: Going public felt sobering, not triumphant; the IPO is the beginning of a harder phase, not the end.
contrarian.zh: 上市带来的感觉是清醒而非喜悦；IPO是更艰难阶段的开始，而非终点。

contrarian.en: Snapchat grows slower than broadcast social media because it is messaging-oriented, spreading through close friends.
contrarian.zh: Snapchat比广播式社交媒体增长更慢，因为它以消息为导向，通过亲密朋友传播。

contrarian.en: Dropping out of Stanford was a calculated risk with minimal downside, not a reckless gamble.
contrarian.zh: 从斯坦福退学是一个经过计算的下行风险极小的决定，而非鲁莽赌博。

contrarian.en: Parents banning TV was an enormous gift, despite making him an outsider among peers.
contrarian.zh: 父母禁止看电视是一份巨大的礼物，尽管这让他在同龄人中显得格格不入。

contrarian.en: Becoming a billionaire mattered less than the earlier moment when investors let him sell stock to buy a house.
contrarian.zh: 成为亿万富翁不如早期投资者允许他出售股票买房那一刻重要。

contrarian.en: He would choose Jeff Bezos over Mark Zuckerberg because Bezos once encouraged him personally when he was young.
contrarian.zh: 他会选择杰夫·贝索斯而非马克·扎克伯格，因为贝索斯曾在他年轻时亲自鼓励他。

transcript.sec: Computing as an accelerant for humanity

turns.en: But also, I think throughout history, even you know, think about Stewart Brand and the Whole Earth Catalog. People who were working on computers in the very, very early days really viewed them as accelerants for humanity, tools for humanity, and talked about them in that way. So I think at its best, computing makes all of us better.
turns.zh: 而且，我想纵观历史，甚至你知道，想想斯图尔特·布兰德和《全球目录》。在最早最早的日子里从事计算机工作的人，真的把它们视为人类的加速器、人类的工具，并且以那种方式谈论它们。所以我认为，在最理想的情况下，计算让我们所有人都变得更好。

turns.en: What's a success that didn't feel as good as you expected?
turns.zh: 有什么成功是你觉得没有想象中那么好的？

turns.en: You know, I think for us, like people always talk about taking the company public, right? And we'd see all these photos and videos, everyone with the confetti coming down and they're ringing the bell and all this kind of thing. And I remember I was meeting with a friend of mine, because I went and talked to a bunch of public company CEOs before we went public, you know, to learn and ask a bunch of questions.
turns.zh: 你知道，我觉得对我们来说，人们总是谈论公司上市，对吧？我们会看到所有这些照片和视频，每个人都在五彩纸屑中，敲响钟声之类的。我记得我在上市前和我的一个朋友见面，因为我去和一群上市公司 CEO 谈过，去学习并问了很多问题。

turns.en: And I remember one of my friends was like, "Whatever you do, do not get the confetti. Tell them no confetti, because every single day from there on out it's hard building a public company. Every single time there's a hiccup or a problem with the company or whatever, they're going to put that confetti photo up."
turns.zh: 我记得我一个朋友说：“无论你做什么，都不要用五彩纸屑。告诉他们不要五彩纸屑，因为从那天起，经营一家上市公司每一天都很艰难。每次公司出现一点小问题或麻烦，他们就会把那张五彩纸屑照片拿出来。”

turns.en: And what was very interesting for me was how sobering that was, right? Because I think so many people view an IPO as an end, right? And in so many ways, it's actually the beginning of a totally different phase for the company, a totally different way of managing and the company communicating about it. So for me, I think that's something that is typically viewed as a success, getting to that milestone, but it comes with so many new responsibilities and so many changes.
turns.zh: 对我而言非常有趣的是，这件事多么令人清醒，对吧？因为我觉得很多人把 IPO 视为终点，对吧？在很多方面，它实际上是公司一个全新阶段的开始，一种完全不同的管理方式和公司沟通方式。所以对我来说，我认为这通常被视为一种成功，达到了那个里程碑，但它伴随着如此多的新责任和如此多的变化。

turns.en: Last quickfire. If you had to go into business with Mark Zuckerberg or Jeff Bezos, who would it be?
turns.zh: 最后一个快问快答。如果你必须和马克·扎克伯格或杰夫·贝索斯一起做生意，你会选谁？

turns.en: Jeff.
turns.zh: 杰夫。

turns.en: Why?
turns.zh: 为什么？

turns.en: Um, because we don't like Mark. You know what, Jeff was really kind to me when I was starting the business. I remember I was in a big executive meeting with Jeff about our Amazon relationship or something like that, and towards the end of the meeting he excused everybody, but he stayed behind with me. And the company was going through a bunch of difficult challenges at the time, and I was really young and just trying to learn how to build the company. And he was like, "Evan, just don't worry about it, just stay focused on what you're doing, you're going to do great."
turns.zh: 嗯，因为我们不喜欢马克。你知道吗，杰夫在我创业时对我非常好。我记得我和杰夫开一个大型高管会议，讨论我们和亚马逊的关系之类的。会议快结束时，他把其他人都打发走了，但单独留了下来。当时公司正经历一系列艰难挑战，我还很年轻，正在努力学习如何经营公司。他说：“埃文，别担心，专注于你正在做的事情，你会做得很好。”

turns.en: And I was like, wow, for him to go out of his way to take that time to connect with me and encourage me like that, it was just a really inspiring thing, and something I've held with me to this day. And I think about that a lot when I meet other founders, right? It's not easy building a company, and for him to go out of his way and just encourage me like that was really powerful.
turns.zh: 我当时想，哇，他能不辞辛劳花时间和我交流，这样鼓励我，这真的是一件非常鼓舞人心的事情，至今仍铭记在心。当我遇到其他创始人时，我经常想到这件事，对吧？经营公司并不容易，他能不辞辛劳这样鼓励我，真的非常有力量。

turns.en: You know, I find that with the entrepreneurial, like the founder community, it's so collaborative, everyone kind of wants to help each other, but also there's competition, right? But people really want to help each other. There are some industries where that doesn't really happen as much, but it's, you know, like Jeff helping you see a young entrepreneur who needs help. That's kind of like the special thing that no one really sees, that goes on behind the scenes, right?
turns.zh: 你知道，我觉得在创业圈，也就是创始人群体里，大家非常合作，每个人都想互相帮助，但也有竞争，对吧？但人们确实很想互相帮助。有些行业这种情况不太常见，但你知道，就像杰夫帮助一个需要帮助的年轻创业者。这就像那种没人真正看到的幕后特殊事情，对吧？

turns.en: I think it is probably the best thing about the technology industry. I mean, I certainly experienced it building our business, and I had the great fortune of knowing absolutely nothing about running a company. So I really relied on all the incredible mentors I met along the way, who were willing to help out or were super responsive if I had a question. And so I do think that that is probably, at least for me, the best part of the industry as a whole.
turns.zh: 我认为这可能是科技行业最好的地方。我的意思是，我在建立自己业务时确实经历过，而且我非常幸运地完全不懂如何经营公司。所以我非常依赖一路上遇到的这些了不起的导师，他们愿意帮忙，或者在我有问题时反应超级迅速。所以我确实认为，至少对我来说，这是整个行业最好的部分。

turns.en: So, where did you grow up?
turns.zh: 那么，你在哪里长大？

turns.en: I grew up in Los Angeles. Yeah. I was raised by two lawyers. My mom was a tax lawyer. My dad did a lot of business litigation. I had two younger sisters, both way smarter than me. And I think, you know, having two lawyers meant for very spirited dinner table conversations, and certainly like debates.
turns.zh: 我在洛杉矶长大。是的。我由两位律师抚养长大。我妈妈是税务律师，我爸爸处理很多商业诉讼。我有两个妹妹，都比我聪明得多。我想，有两个律师意味着晚餐桌上会有非常热烈的对话，当然还有辩论。

turns.en: Yeah, debates and never, you know, never averse to conflict, right? I mean, lawyers actually, I think, in some ways feed off conflict. And so, I think it was really interesting to grow up in an environment where there was a real commitment to intellectual honesty and integrity. I mean, we used to call my dad, you know, the encyclopedia before Google came along and sort of unseated him from his position of knowing so much about the world, really passionate about history and economics. And so there would just be really great and intense debates around the table in our home growing up.
turns.zh: 是的，辩论，而且永远不会，你知道，永远不会回避冲突，对吧？我的意思是，律师实际上，我认为，在某些方面以冲突为生。所以，我觉得在一个真正致力于智识诚实和正直的环境中长大非常有趣。我的意思是，在谷歌出现并把他从这个位置上赶下来之前，我们过去常叫我爸爸“百科全书”，他对历史和经济学非常热衷。所以在我们家里，餐桌上总是有非常精彩而激烈的辩论。

turns.en: What does that teach you, though?
turns.zh: 但这教会了你什么？

turns.en: You know, I think one of the things that taught me at a very young age was the ability to stand my ground in really tough conversations. I mean, I remember getting to know my wife, and like, us all having dinner with my dad or something, and I'm just debating with my dad, and my wife's like, "What are you doing?" Like, I'm like, "No, this is like our love language," like, we're having a conversation. But I think it was really fun to be in an environment that encouraged that, because I think that sort of intellectual curiosity and spirited debate is so much at the heart of creating good ideas. And that's really valuable.
turns.zh: 你知道，我认为这在我很小的时候教会我的一件事，就是在非常艰难的对话中坚持自己立场的能力。我的意思是，我记得认识我妻子的时候，比如我们和我爸爸一起吃晚饭什么的，我就在和我爸爸辩论，我妻子说：“你在干什么？”我说：“不，这就像我们的爱的语言”，我们只是在聊天。但我认为，身处一个鼓励这种氛围的环境真的很有趣，因为我认为那种智识上的好奇心和激烈的辩论正是产生好想法的核心。这真的非常有价值。

turns.en: Yeah, I've never thought of it that way, because you have to—life is sometimes about having those hard conversations and also being able to stand your ground. I think that's in some ways really what separates good leaders from great leaders, and that has to be from childhood.
turns.zh: 是的，我从未这样想过，因为你必须——生活有时就是要进行那些艰难的对话，并且能够坚持自己的立场。我认为这在某种程度上确实是区分优秀领导者和伟大领导者的东西，而这必须从童年开始。

turns.en: But also to develop at the same time a willingness to be open-minded when you're wrong, right? And I think that's where that focus on intellectual integrity is so important, because the dinner table was about getting to the right answer, not being right. And that was a really interesting dynamic.
turns.zh: 但同时也要培养一种当你错了时愿意保持开放心态的态度，对吧？我认为这就是对智识诚实如此重视的原因，因为餐桌上的目标是得出正确的答案，而不是非要自己对。这是一个非常有趣的动态。

turns.en: So you stubborn I can be? Yeah, I can be.
turns.zh: 所以你可以很固执？是的，我可以。

turns.en: But if you know you're wrong, you admit you're wrong, or you will hold?
turns.zh: 但如果你知道自己错了，你会承认错误，还是会坚持？

turns.en: To me, the entire game is how quickly can you change your mind once you find out you're wrong.
turns.zh: 对我来说，整个关键就在于，一旦你发现自己错了，你能多快改变主意。

turns.en: So give me an example. What do you mean?
turns.zh: 那给我举个例子。你是什么意思？

turns.en: I think, you know, for example, when we're working on a new product in our company, or I'm really holding my ground on a feature, as soon as somebody proves I'm wrong, or shows me our customers are looking for something different, or has a better idea...
turns.zh: 我想，例如，当我们在公司开发新产品时，或者我对某个功能非常坚持，一旦有人证明我错了，或者向我展示我们的客户在寻找不同的东西，或者有更好的想法……
